title: Variance and generic math
sub: out T, in T and INumber<T>
cards/0/title: Why List<string> is not a List<object>
cards/0/body: If that assignment were allowed, you could put a number into a list of strings through the "list of objects" — and break it.
cards/0/code:
List<object> objs = new List<string>();   // compile error
objs.Add(42);                              // and this is why
cards/1/body: IEnumerable<T>, on the other hand, only hands out T and never takes one in. So a sequence of strings can safely be treated as a sequence of objects. That is marked with out: IEnumerable<out T>.
cards/2/body: Action<in T> only takes in T. An action that can print any object also works where an action for string is expected.
cards/2/code:
Action<object> print = o => Console.WriteLine(o);
Action<string> printText = print;   // allowed
cards/3/explain: IList takes elements in (Add), so it is invariant.
cards/5/body: Arrays have been covariant since .NET 1.0 — before generics existed. The compiler lets this through, and it fails at run time:
cards/6/body: You used to be unable to write Sum<T> for any number type: T has no + operator. Now interfaces can require static members, and INumber<T> gives you +, −, Zero and the rest.
cards/7/q: A sum for any number type
cards/7/explain: Zero is a static property from the interface, so you write T.Zero.
cards/8/q: Why does the compiler accept object[] arr = new string[2], even though it is risky?
cards/8/options/0: Array covariance stayed from .NET 1.0 for compatibility; the check happens at run time
cards/8/explain: Generic interfaces made variance safe, but arrays stayed as they were.
